meta.title: Four Gospels, one Jesus
meta.uniqueSource: Approximate share of each Gospel found in no other Gospel, as calculated by B. F. Westcott, Introduction to the Study of the Gospels (1860), and widely quoted since.
meta.orderNote: Events follow a traditional harmony of the Gospels. The writers sometimes group events by theme rather than strict time order, so the exact sequence of some events is uncertain.

gospels.name: Matthew
gospels.portraitLong: Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of David, who fulfils the Law and the Prophets and brings the kingdom of heaven.
gospels.author: Matthew (Levi), the apostle
gospels.authorBio: A tax collector in Capernaum whom Jesus called to follow him (Matthew 9:9). Tax collectors worked for Rome and were despised by their own people, so Matthew knew what it meant to be welcomed by grace. As one of the Twelve he was an eyewitness of much of what he records. The book does not name its author, but the early church, from Papias (c. AD 120) onward, consistently names Matthew.
gospels.readersLong: Matthew writes for readers who know the Old Testament well. He does not explain Jewish customs, and he often says “kingdom of heaven” where the other Gospels say “kingdom of God”, following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding God's name.
gospels.purpose: To show that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the true King of Israel, and that his kingdom is now open to all nations.
gospels.styleLong: Matthew arranges his material carefully. Narrative sections alternate with five great blocks of Jesus' teaching, and he returns again and again to the words “this was to fulfil what the Lord had spoken by the prophet”.
gospels.opens: With a genealogy from Abraham through King David
gospels.ends: With the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations

firstWords.text: The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

lastWords.text: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.

keyVerse.text: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.

distinctives: More Old Testament quotations than any other Gospel
Five great teaching blocks: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the mission of the Twelve (10), parables of the kingdom (13), life in the community of disciples (18) and the end of the age (24–25)
The only Gospel to use the word “church” (16:18; 18:17)
The visit of the wise men and the escape to Egypt
Peter walking on the water, and the guard at the tomb
Parables found only here, including the ten virgins and the sheep and the goats

gospels.name: Mark
gospels.portraitLong: Jesus is the powerful Son of God who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
gospels.author: John Mark, with Peter
gospels.authorBio: John Mark grew up in Jerusalem, where the church met in his mother's house (Acts 12:12). He was Barnabas's cousin and set out with Paul and Barnabas on their first journey, but turned back (Acts 13:13). Later he was restored and became “very useful” to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter calls him “my son” (1 Peter 5:13). Early writers, beginning with Papias, say Mark wrote down Peter's preaching about Jesus.
gospels.readersLong: Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them (7:3-4) and translates Aramaic words such as “Talitha cumi” (5:41). Christians in Rome were beginning to suffer for their faith, and Mark shows them a Saviour who suffered first.
gospels.purpose: To show who Jesus is through what he did, and to call readers to follow him on the way of the cross.
gospels.styleLong: The shortest Gospel moves quickly. The word “immediately” appears more than forty times, and Mark includes small eyewitness details: the cushion in the boat, the green grass, Jesus' looks and feelings. About a third of the book is given to the last week of Jesus' life.
gospels.opens: Straight into the ministry of John the Baptist, with no birth story
gospels.ends: At the empty tomb, with the women trembling and amazed

firstWords.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

lastWords.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.

gospels.lastNote: The earliest manuscripts end at 16:8. Verses 9-20 are found in most later manuscripts and are printed in brackets in the ESV.

keyVerse.text: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

distinctives: The shortest Gospel, and full of action rather than long speeches
Translates Aramaic words Jesus spoke, such as “Talitha cumi” (5:41) and “Ephphatha” (7:34)
Often notes Jesus' emotions: compassion, anger, sighing, love (1:41; 3:5; 8:12; 10:21)
The “Messianic secret”: Jesus often tells people not to spread who he is
Two healings found only here: a deaf man (7:31-37) and a blind man healed in two stages (8:22-26)
A young man who fled naked at Jesus' arrest (14:51-52), often thought to be Mark himself

gospels.name: Luke
gospels.portraitLong: Jesus is the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost: the poor, women, outcasts, sinners and Gentiles.
gospels.author: Luke, the doctor
gospels.authorBio: Luke was a physician (Colossians 4:14) and Paul's travelling companion; the “we” passages of Acts show him on the road with Paul. He was most likely a Gentile, the only non-Jewish writer of the New Testament. He was not an eyewitness himself, but he carefully investigated everything from the beginning, talking with those who were (Luke 1:1-4). He also wrote Acts, the second volume of the same work.
gospels.readersLong: Luke addresses “most excellent Theophilus”, probably a Roman official or wealthy believer, so that he may have certainty about what he has been taught. He dates events by Roman rulers and traces Jesus' family line back to Adam, not only to Abraham.
gospels.purpose: To write an orderly, well-researched account so that readers can be certain of the truth about Jesus.
gospels.styleLong: Luke writes the most polished Greek of the Gospels. He anchors events in world history (2:1-2; 3:1-2) and gives a long travel narrative as Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem (9:51–19:27). He has a special eye for prayer, the Holy Spirit, joy, and people others overlooked.
gospels.opens: With a preface to Theophilus, then the births of John and Jesus
gospels.ends: With Jesus' ascension and the disciples worshipping with great joy

firstWords.text: It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.

lastWords.text: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.

keyVerse.text: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

distinctives: The longest Gospel, and the fullest account of Jesus' birth and childhood
Four songs of praise: Mary's (1:46-55), Zechariah's (1:68-79), the angels' (2:14) and Simeon's (2:29-32)
Many parables found only here, such as the good Samaritan and the lost son
Shows Jesus praying at key moments: his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, at the transfiguration, on the cross
Gives special place to women, the poor, Samaritans and tax collectors
The only Gospel to describe the ascension (24:50-53)

items.label: The lost coin and the lost son
The Pharisee and the tax collector

gospels.name: John
gospels.portraitLong: Jesus is the eternal Word who was with God and was God, who became flesh so that all who believe in him may have life.
gospels.author: John, the apostle
gospels.authorBio: A Galilean fisherman, son of Zebedee and brother of James. With Peter and James he was one of Jesus' closest three, present at the transfiguration and in Gethsemane. The Gospel's author calls himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20-24), and he stood at the cross, where Jesus entrusted his mother to him. Early writers, especially Irenaeus, say John wrote it late in his life at Ephesus.
gospels.readers: The wider church, Jews and Greeks
gospels.readersLong: Writing decades after the other Gospels, John assumes his readers already know the main story. He explains Jewish feasts and Hebrew words for a wide audience, and writes so that both seekers and believers may believe and keep believing.
gospels.purpose: “That you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name” (20:31).
gospels.styleLong: John uses simple words for deep truths, and strong contrasts: light and darkness, life and death, truth and lies. Instead of short sayings and parables, he records long conversations and speeches, and he chooses seven signs that reveal who Jesus is. Most of his Gospel is set in Judea and Jerusalem rather than Galilee.
gospels.opens: Before creation: “In the beginning was the Word”
gospels.ends: With Peter restored and the beloved disciple's testimony

firstWords.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

lastWords.text: Now there are also many other things that Jesus did. Were every one of them to be written, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.

keyVerse.text: but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

distinctives: Seven signs and seven “I am” sayings that reveal who Jesus is
Mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is why we speak of a three-year ministry
No parables in the usual sense and no casting out of demons
Long conversations with individuals: Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, Martha, Pilate
Five chapters on the night before the cross: the foot washing and Jesus' farewell teaching (13–17)
The raising of Lazarus, and Jesus' meeting with Thomas

items.label: I am the bread of life
I am the light of the world
I am the door of the sheep
I am the resurrection and the life
I am the way, and the truth, and the life
A paralysed man healed at the pool

phases.label: Birth and early years
phases.about: Only Matthew and Luke tell of Jesus' birth, Matthew from Joseph's side and Luke from Mary's. John begins before time itself.

phases.label: Preparation
phases.about: John the Baptist prepares the way, and Jesus is baptised and tempted.

phases.label: Early ministry
phases.about: A first year that only John records, much of it in Judea and Samaria.

phases.label: Ministry in Galilee
phases.about: Teaching, healing and calling disciples around the Sea of Galilee. Most of what the first three Gospels share is here.

phases.label: Toward Jerusalem
phases.about: Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem. Luke's long travel section and John's visits to the feasts fill this period.

phases.label: The last week
phases.about: From the entry into Jerusalem to the upper room.

phases.label: Arrest, trial and the cross
phases.about: The one part of the story all four Gospels tell in full.

phases.label: Resurrection and ascension
phases.about: Each writer chooses different appearances of the risen Lord. Together they give a fuller picture than any one alone.

events.title: Jesus' family line

details.mt: Begins with Abraham and comes down through David and Solomon to Joseph, in three sets of fourteen generations.
details.lk: Goes backward from Jesus through David's son Nathan all the way to “Adam, the son of God”.

events.note: The two lists differ between David and Joseph. Many evangelical scholars think Matthew gives Joseph's royal, legal line and Luke gives Mary's family line (or Joseph's natural line).

events.title: The angel Gabriel comes to Mary

details.mt: Told from Joseph's side: an angel speaks to him in a dream, and the child is called Immanuel, “God with us”.
details.lk: Told from Mary's side: the census of Caesar Augustus brings them to Bethlehem, and the baby is laid in a manger.

events.title: Presented in the temple: Simeon and Anna
Escape to Egypt and home to Nazareth
Jesus at twelve in the temple
John the Baptist prepares the way

details.mt: John warns the Pharisees and Sadducees: “Bear fruit in keeping with repentance.”
details.mk: Brief and direct: John's camel's-hair clothing, his diet of locusts and wild honey, and the promise of one mightier who will baptise with the Holy Spirit.
details.lk: Dates John's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and records his practical advice to crowds, tax collectors and soldiers.
details.jn: John says plainly that he is not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet, but “the voice of one crying out in the wilderness”.

details.mt: John at first refuses: “I need to be baptized by you.” The Father speaks about Jesus: “This is my beloved Son.”
details.mk: The heavens are “torn open”, and the Father speaks to Jesus directly: “You are my beloved Son.”
details.lk: Heaven opens while Jesus is praying, and the Spirit descends “in bodily form, like a dove”.
details.jn: Does not describe the baptism itself. John the Baptist testifies that he saw the Spirit come down and remain on Jesus, and calls him “the Lamb of God”.

details.mt: Three temptations, ending on a very high mountain with the kingdoms of the world. Angels then minister to Jesus.
details.mk: Just two verses, but only Mark says Jesus “was with the wild animals”.
details.lk: The same three temptations, but ending at the temple in Jerusalem. The devil leaves “until an opportune time”.

events.title: The first disciples meet Jesus
events.note: Andrew, Peter, Philip and Nathanael first meet Jesus here. The call to leave their nets, in the other Gospels, comes later.

events.title: Water turned into wine at Cana
Clearing the temple (John)
events.note: The other Gospels record a clearing of the temple in the last week. Many evangelical scholars believe Jesus did this twice, at the start and end of his ministry; others think John placed one event early for teaching reasons.

events.title: Rejected in his home town, Nazareth

details.mt: The people ask, “Is not this the carpenter's son?”
details.mk: They ask, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?” Jesus “could do no mighty work there” and marvels at their unbelief.
details.lk: Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled.” The crowd tries to throw him off a cliff.

events.note: Luke places this at the start of the Galilean ministry, Matthew and Mark later. It may have been two separate visits.

details.mt: Peter and Andrew, then James and John, leave their nets “immediately”.
details.mk: James and John leave their father Zebedee in the boat “with the hired servants”.
details.lk: Comes after a miraculous catch of fish. Peter falls at Jesus' knees: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”

events.title: An unclean spirit driven out at Capernaum

details.mt: Links Jesus' healings to Isaiah 53: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.”
details.mk: Jesus “took her by the hand and lifted her up”.
details.lk: Luke the doctor says it was a “high fever”, and that Jesus “rebuked the fever”.

details.mk: Jesus is “moved with pity” as he touches him. The man spreads the news so widely that Jesus can no longer openly enter a town.
details.lk: The man is “full of leprosy”. Afterwards Jesus withdraws to desolate places to pray.

events.title: A paralysed man forgiven and healed

details.mt: Does not mention the roof. The crowds glorify God, “who had given such authority to men”.
details.mk: Four friends dig through the roof to lower him down.
details.lk: They let him down “through the tiles”, and Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village to listen.

details.mt: Matthew tells his own story and calls himself “Matthew”. Jesus quotes Hosea: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.”
details.mk: Calls him “Levi the son of Alphaeus”.
details.lk: Levi “left everything” and holds a great feast for Jesus in his house.

events.title: A paralysed man healed at the pool of Bethesda
events.note: This happens on a visit to Jerusalem for a feast, during the time of the Galilean ministry.

details.mk: Only Mark adds: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”

events.title: A man with a withered hand healed

details.mk: Jesus looks around at them “with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart”.
details.lk: Notes it was the man's right hand.

events.title: The twelve apostles chosen

details.mt: Lists the Twelve in pairs and calls himself “Matthew the tax collector”.
details.mk: Jesus gives James and John the name “Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder”.
details.lk: Jesus spends the whole night in prayer before choosing them.

events.note: The lists match except that Thaddaeus (Matthew, Mark) is called “Judas the son of James” by Luke: one man with two names.

events.title: The Sermon on the Mount / on the Plain

details.mt: Three chapters on a mountain, beginning with the Beatitudes: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”
details.lk: Shorter, “on a level place”, with four blessings and four woes: “Blessed are you who are poor.”

events.note: Some see one sermon told two ways; many think Luke records a similar sermon on another occasion. Jesus surely taught the same things more than once.

events.title: The Lord's Prayer

details.mt: Part of the Sermon on the Mount: “Pray then like this.”
details.lk: A shorter form, given when a disciple asks, “Lord, teach us to pray.”

events.note: Luke places this later, on the journey to Jerusalem, so Jesus probably taught the prayer on more than one occasion.

events.title: A centurion's servant healed

details.mt: The centurion comes to Jesus. Jesus says many will come from east and west to the feast of the kingdom.
details.lk: The centurion sends Jewish elders and then friends, who say he loves the nation and built their synagogue.

events.note: Not a contradiction: as with a letter sent by a king, people spoke for the centurion through his messengers.

events.title: A widow's son raised at Nain
A sinful woman anoints Jesus' feet
events.note: A different event from the anointing at Bethany in the last week.

events.title: The seed that grows by itself

details.mt: The disciples pray: “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.”
details.mk: Jesus is asleep “on the cushion” in the stern. “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”
details.lk: “Master, Master, we are perishing!”

events.title: Demons cast out into the pigs

details.mt: Mentions two men.
details.mk: The fullest account. The man's name is Legion; afterwards he begs to go with Jesus but is sent home to tell what the Lord has done.
details.lk: The healed man is found “sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind”.

events.note: Mark and Luke focus on one man, perhaps the more prominent of the two Matthew mentions.

events.title: Jairus's daughter and the woman who touched his cloak

details.mt: The shortest version.
details.mk: The woman had suffered under many physicians and “grew worse”. Jesus says to the girl, “Talitha cumi”.
details.lk: Luke the doctor puts it more kindly: she “could not be healed by anyone”. Notes the girl was an only daughter, about twelve.

details.mt: Followed by a long block of teaching on mission and persecution (10:16-42).
details.mk: Sent out “two by two”.
The fullest account: Herod feared John and “heard him gladly”, until Herodias's daughter danced at his birthday banquet.
details.lk: Only Herod's question: “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?”

events.title: Five thousand fed

details.mt: “About five thousand men, besides women and children.”
details.mk: Jesus has compassion on them “because they were like sheep without a shepherd”, and they sit in groups “on the green grass”.
details.lk: Places it near Bethsaida and follows it directly with Peter's confession.
details.jn: A boy gives five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd want to make Jesus king by force, and the next day he teaches, “I am the bread of life.”

events.note: Apart from the resurrection, this is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.

details.mt: Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water and beginning to sink. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”
details.mk: Jesus “meant to pass by them”. The disciples are astonished, “for their hearts were hardened”.
details.jn: When they take him into the boat, “immediately the boat was at the land”.

events.title: “I am the bread of life”
events.note: Many disciples turn away after this teaching. Peter answers, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

details.mt: Calls her “a Canaanite woman”, and she cries, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David.”
details.mk: Calls her “a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth”.

events.title: A blind man healed in two stages
Peter's confession: “You are the Christ”

details.mt: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus answers, “On this rock I will build my church.”
details.mk: Simply, “You are the Christ.”
details.lk: “The Christ of God.” Jesus had been praying alone.

events.note: Compare Peter's words in John 6:68-69: “You are the Holy One of God.”

details.mt: Peter rebukes Jesus, and Jesus answers, “Get behind me, Satan!”
details.mk: Jesus “said this plainly”, and rebukes Peter while looking at the disciples.
details.lk: Says we must take up our cross “daily”.

events.title: The transfiguration

details.mt: His face “shone like the sun”. The terrified disciples fall down, and Jesus touches them: “Rise, and have no fear.”
details.mk: His clothes became “radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them”.
details.lk: It happens while Jesus is praying. Moses and Elijah speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem”.

events.note: Peter recalls it in 2 Peter 1:16-18, and John may echo it: “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14).

events.title: A boy with an unclean spirit healed

details.mk: The father's cry: “I believe; help my unbelief!”

events.title: The coin in the fish's mouth
At the Feast of Booths: “Come to me and drink”
The lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son

details.mt: Only the lost sheep, told to the disciples about caring for “these little ones”.
details.lk: Three parables in a row, told to grumbling Pharisees, each ending in joy over one sinner who repents.

events.title: The Pharisee and the tax collector

details.mk: Jesus is “indignant” with the disciples, and takes the children in his arms.

details.mt: Tells us he was young.
details.mk: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him.”
details.lk: Tells us he was a ruler.

events.title: Blind Bartimaeus at Jericho

details.mt: Mentions two blind men.
details.mk: Gives his name, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus. He throws off his cloak and springs up.
details.lk: Places it as Jesus draws near to Jericho.

events.note: Matthew and Mark say Jesus was leaving Jericho; Luke says he was approaching it. There were an old and a new Jericho close together, which may explain this.

events.title: Jesus anointed at Bethany

details.mt: “A woman” pours the ointment on his head; the disciples object to the waste.
details.mk: The nard is worth more than three hundred denarii, about a year's wages.
details.jn: Names her as Mary, sister of Lazarus. She anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair, and Judas objects because he was a thief.

events.note: John dates it six days before the Passover. Matthew and Mark tell it later, beside Judas's betrayal, perhaps to contrast her devotion with his.

details.mt: Quotes Zechariah 9:9 and mentions both a donkey and her colt. “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
details.mk: A colt “on which no one has ever sat”. “Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!”
details.lk: “If these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” Jesus weeps over Jerusalem.
details.jn: The only Gospel to mention palm branches. The crowd had heard he raised Lazarus.

events.title: Clearing the temple

details.mt: Jesus heals the blind and lame in the temple, and children shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
details.mk: Quotes Isaiah in full: “a house of prayer for all the nations”.
details.lk: Very brief, followed by Jesus teaching daily in the temple.

events.note: John records a clearing of the temple at the start of the ministry (John 2:13-22).

events.title: The greatest commandment

details.mk: The scribe agrees with Jesus, who tells him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

events.note: In Luke 10:25-28 a lawyer gives the same two commandments, which leads to the good Samaritan.

events.title: Teaching on the end of the age

details.mt: The longest version, followed by parables of the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and the goats.
details.lk: Speaks of Jerusalem “surrounded by armies”, fulfilled when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70.

details.mt: Only Matthew gives the price: thirty pieces of silver.
details.lk: “Satan entered into Judas.” (Compare John 13:27.)

events.title: The Last Supper

details.mt: The cup is “poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins”.
details.mk: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”
details.lk: Two cups, and the words “Do this in remembrance of me.” Afterwards the disciples argue about who is greatest.
details.jn: Does not record the bread and cup. John focuses on Jesus identifying the betrayer and on the teaching around the meal.

events.note: Paul also records the Lord's Supper in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26.

events.title: The farewell teaching and Jesus' prayer
events.note: Four chapters of teaching on the Holy Spirit, abiding in the vine, and love, ending with Jesus' prayer for his disciples and for all who will believe.

events.title: Praying in Gethsemane

details.mt: Jesus prays three times, “not as I will, but as you will”.
details.mk: Jesus prays, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you.”
details.lk: An angel strengthens him, and his sweat becomes like great drops of blood.

events.note: John names the garden (18:1) but goes straight to the arrest.

details.mt: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword.” Jesus could call on twelve legions of angels.
details.mk: A young man in a linen cloth flees naked, a detail often taken as Mark's own signature.
details.lk: Jesus heals the servant's ear.
details.jn: Names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant. When Jesus says “I am he”, the soldiers fall to the ground.

events.title: Before the high priest and the council

details.mt: Caiaphas demands under oath: “Tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.”
details.mk: Jesus answers plainly, “I am,” and speaks of the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.
details.lk: Adds a formal council meeting at daybreak.
details.jn: Jesus is first questioned by Annas, Caiaphas's father-in-law.

details.mt: Peter's Galilean accent gives him away.
details.mk: The rooster crows twice, as Jesus had said, a detail Peter himself would remember.
details.lk: “The Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
details.jn: Another disciple, known to the high priest, brings Peter into the courtyard. A relative of Malchus recognises him.

events.title: Judas's remorse and death
events.note: Acts 1:18-19 also describes Judas's death and the field bought with the money.

details.mt: Jesus gives no answer to the charges, “so that the governor was greatly amazed”.
details.mk: Pilate asks, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus answers, “You have said so.”
details.lk: Lists the charges: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, claiming to be a king. Pilate says, “I find no guilt in this man.”
details.jn: A private conversation: “My kingdom is not of this world.” Pilate asks, “What is truth?”

details.mt: Pilate's wife warns him after a dream, and Pilate washes his hands before the crowd.
details.mk: Pilate hands Jesus over, “wishing to satisfy the crowd”.
details.lk: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times.
details.jn: Pilate presents Jesus crowned with thorns: “Behold the man!” The chief priests answer, “We have no king but Caesar.”

details.mt: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross. The chief priests mock: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now.”
details.mk: Simon of Cyrene is “the father of Alexander and Rufus”, men Mark's readers seem to have known.
details.lk: Two sayings from the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” and, to the thief who repents, “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
details.jn: Jesus goes out “bearing his own cross”. The sign is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek. Jesus gives his mother into the care of the beloved disciple: “Behold, your mother!”

events.title: The death of Jesus

details.mt: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” The earth shakes, the temple curtain is torn, and tombs are opened.
details.mk: The same cry in Aramaic, “Eloi, Eloi…” The centurion says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”
details.lk: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” The centurion says, “Certainly this man was innocent!”
details.jn: “I thirst” and “It is finished.” A soldier pierces his side, and blood and water flow out.

events.note: Together the Gospels record seven sayings from the cross. No single Gospel has more than three.

details.mt: Joseph of Arimathea, “a rich man”, lays Jesus in his own new tomb.
details.mk: Joseph “took courage” to ask for the body, and Pilate checks that Jesus is already dead.
details.lk: Joseph had not agreed with the council's decision. The women prepare spices.
details.jn: Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes.

events.title: The guard at the tomb
events.note: Matthew alone records the sealed tomb and the guards later bribed to say the disciples stole the body.

events.title: The empty tomb

details.mt: An earthquake; an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it, and the guards become like dead men.
details.mk: The young man in white says, “Go, tell his disciples and Peter.” The women flee in fear.
details.lk: Two men in dazzling clothes: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?”
details.jn: Mary Magdalene runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who race to the tomb and find the face cloth folded up by itself.

events.note: The accounts name different women and different numbers of angels. They complement each other: none says that only one woman or one angel was there.

events.title: Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and the women

details.mt: Jesus meets the women on the way, and they take hold of his feet and worship him.
details.jn: Mary thinks he is the gardener, until he calls her by name: “Mary.”

events.note: The longer ending of Mark (16:9-11) also mentions this appearance.

events.title: On the road to Emmaus
events.note: The longer ending of Mark (16:12-13) also mentions this appearance.

details.lk: Jesus eats broiled fish in front of them and opens their minds to understand the Scriptures.
details.jn: He shows them his hands and side, and breathes on them: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

events.title: Breakfast by the lake; Peter restored
The Great Commission
events.note: Luke 24:46-49 and John 20:21 also record Jesus sending out his disciples, in different words.

events.title: The ascension
events.note: Luke tells the story again at the start of Acts (1:9-11). The longer ending of Mark (16:19) also mentions it.
